Issued at 1038 PM MDT Fri Sep 11 2026

WINDY AND WARM WITH ISOLATED STORMS THIS WEEKEND:

Modest moisture has settled in over the region, promoting 
sparse, weak showers and thunderstorms over Colorado's west 
slope. This comes amidst warm zonal upper-level flow set up 
across the majority of the western CONUS. Decent mixing 
underneath the strong flow paired with a modest pressure 
gradient has supported and will continue to support gusty 
afternoon winds. In addition, with low- levels on the drier 
side, showers will also contribute to windy conditions should 
gusty outflow winds develop. Over the next 48 hours as moisture 
continues to creep upwards, look for storms to increase in 
coverage, particularly over the high terrain. Impacts should 
remain relatively isolated Saturday, but we could see storm 
coverage become more scattered on Sunday as the next strong push
of moisture begins to move in.

COOLER AND WETTER PATTERN MONDAY AND BEYOND:

As we begin the work week, a powerful trough will push into the
PacNW, pushing flow across the southwestern CONUS to 
southwesterly. This pulls subtropical moisture further inland 
towards us. As such, by Monday, look for the strong plume of 
moisture to be centered over the CWA. PWAT anomalies are 
anticipated to be near or exceed 200% of normal on Monday, 
pushing or breaking records for this time of year. The ECMWF Ens
is more bullish on the moisture, but even the GFS Ens is 
indicating PWAT's should be a sure-thing to exceed the 75th 
percentile. Either way, this pool of moisture surging through 
the region will be enough to prompt our next round of widespread
showers and thunderstorms.

With mid-level moisture already in place and only strengthening
over the coming days, cloud cover should generally be ample, 
including in the morning. This will dampen storm potential, 
potentially enough to push storm mode more in a stratiform 
direction. However, dynamic forcing looks to be on the more 
favorable side with this system, perhaps the most impressive 
that we've seen in weeks. For one, by Monday we are expected to 
fall underneath the right entrance region of a powerful jet. In 
addition to jet placement, overnight Sunday into Monday morning 
look for cold front pass through. Both factors will go towards 
supporting discrete storm development. With this, at the very 
least we should expect to see embedded stronger storms in 
stratiform rainfall, if not widespread discrete storm 
development. Wherever discrete storms do develop (whether they 
be isolated or widespread in nature), localized heavy rainfall 
will also be likely, especially in areas where the low-level 
atmosphere is able to significantly moisten up over the weekend.
As far as QPF goes, the NBM is heavily favoring southwestern-
facing slopes of the San Juans, Grand Mesa, and West Elk 
Mountains. In these locations, the NBM probability of exceeding 
a half inch of rain Monday is over 75%, though this could be an 
overestimate if rain stratiforms out. Northeastern-facing slopes
are expected to see lower rain totals, though with a quarter 
inch of precipitation still likely according to the NBM (>50% 
chance), hydrologic concerns would still be on the table. That 
being said, with a few days left to go until the event, it is 
key to understand that there are too many uncertain factors left
to be figured out before we can speculate on the likeliest 
scenario. Stay tuned for future updates, especially once we 
receive hi-res model guidance.

Though the combination of highly anomalous moisture and 
reasonably strong forcing is most potent on Monday, active 
weather looks to stay relatively strong throughout the work 
week. The pool of moisture looks to lock in over the West Slope,
and the jet continues to stretch across the Intermountain West.
Without a clear frontal boundary or shortwave accompanying the 
mid-to-late week pattern, impacts could become even more 
conditional on morning cloud cover, but that is a problem that 
we cannot resolve at this point in time. Ensembles are in step 
with each other that moisture dissipates on Friday, but even 
then there is no indication that we will see PWAT's fall below 
normal, so look for a weakening in storms, but not a complete 
dissipation.
